request: Custom scorers written with the scorer decorator carry their function source code, and loading one runs that code. Today this happens inside the tracking server itself, for example when a scorer is invoked, when online-scoring settings are validated, and when gateway guardrails are loaded. That means user-supplied code can run in the server process, which is a security problem. Desired behavior: the server must never execute custom scorer code. In the server, a custom scorer should load as inert metadata that keeps its fields and serialized form, so it can be inspected and passed along to the job executor, but running it must raise an error. The job executor should still rebuild and run custom scorers as before, and a regular client process, such as a user loading a registered scorer to run locally, should behave exactly as it does now. This refusal must be enforced at the point where scorers are rebuilt, so a future code path in the server can't bypass it, and the server must not be able to pick up executor permission from its surrounding environment. Gateway guardrails run inside the server, so custom decorator-based scorers must be rejected as guardrails, both when a guardrail is created and when one is loaded. This includes ensembles that contain a custom scorer. Built-in scorers and judges created with the judge-making helper must keep working. If an endpoint already has a guardrail backed by a custom scorer, requests to it should fail with a server error that names the guardrail, instead of silently skipping it and serving traffic unprotected. Other guardrail loading failures should still be skipped and logged as they are now. A custom scorer refused as a guardrail raises `UnsupportedGuardrailScorerError`, defined in `mlflow.gateway.guardrails`.

request: When the AI Gateway streams a response containing multiple parallel tool calls through the Gemini or LiteLLM providers, every tool call is reported with the same position (index 0). Clients that assemble streamed tool calls by index then merge separate calls into one, concatenating their arguments into a single broken call. For Gemini, each tool call arrives whole, so two calls in the same streamed chunk both show index 0, and calls arriving in later chunks also restart at 0. For LiteLLM, the index that the underlying library supplies on each chunk is ignored and replaced with the call's position within that chunk, so interleaved chunks for call 0 and call 1 all end up as 0. Desired behavior: for Gemini, tool calls should get consecutive indices across the whole stream, so calls in one chunk are numbered 0, 1, and so on, and calls in later chunks continue the numbering. For LiteLLM, the index provided on each streamed chunk should be preserved, falling back to the call's position in the chunk only when none is provided. That way, arguments for each call are merged correctly per index. Two issues are out of scope: Gemini's finish reason never reporting tool calls, and the Bedrock index offset after a text block.

request: On a registered model that uses stages, loading a model through the "latest" alias form (model name followed by @latest) can return a different version than loading it through the "latest" path form (model name followed by /latest). For example, if a model has versions 1 and 2 and version 2 is moved to the Production stage, the path form loads version 2 but the alias form loads version 1, the older version still in stage None. The alias appears to pick whichever version comes first among the per-stage latest versions, which isn't necessarily the highest version once the model spans more than one stage. The reserved "latest" alias should always resolve to the highest version number of the model, regardless of how many stages are in use or which order they come in. This should match what the path form already returns, so the two forms agree in every case. One consequence is that if the highest version is archived (for example version 1 in Production and version 2 in Archived), the alias now returns version 2, as the path form already does. Models without stages, such as prompts, already behave correctly and should be unaffected.

request: When I stream a response through the AI Gateway's Anthropic provider and the model makes parallel tool calls, the calls get merged into one. Every tool call is reported with index 0, the second call is placed in the second choice instead of the first, and the finish event is sent once per content block instead of once at the end. Clients that read only the first choice and merge tool-call fragments by index (such as the OpenAI Python client and LangChain) end up with a single tool call whose arguments are the concatenation of both calls' arguments. The same problem can occur when a text block comes before a tool call, because the tool call's position then depends on the text block's position. Streaming should number tool calls sequentially from 0 in the order they appear, regardless of any text blocks before them. Every streamed chunk should use only the first choice. The finish event should be emitted exactly once per response. Non-streaming behavior should stay as it is.

request: Copying or serializing trace data fails today. Calling a deep copy or pickle on a finalized (immutable) span raises an error saying a thread lock cannot be pickled. A span loaded lazily from a stored trace produces a broken copy that errors with a missing internal key when inspected. Because traces fetched through the get-trace or search-traces APIs contain these lazy spans, deep-copying or pickling a whole trace also fails, which breaks multiprocessing and other process-based distributed pipelines. Deep copy and pickle should work for immutable spans, lazily loaded spans, no-op spans, and whole traces, and the restored objects should keep the same data, including any attachments. A restored lazy span should stay unloaded until its data is first accessed, and the pickled payload should not carry duplicate raw data. A shallow copy of an immutable span should keep working and share the underlying span. A span that is still live and being recorded should refuse deep copy and pickle with a clear error telling the user to convert it to an immutable span first, while a shallow copy of a live span should keep working.

request: Metric queries that combine pre-aggregated trace rollup data with raw metrics can fail when the rollup sums come back as exact decimal numbers while the raw metric sums come back as floating-point numbers. The two types can't be merged, so the query errors out instead of returning results. The desired behavior is that these queries always succeed, with the sums converted to a compatible numeric type before being combined. Separately, trace search and rollup maintenance put more load on the database than necessary. Sorting traces by attributes that can never be empty shouldn't add extra handling for empty values, though optional fields must still sort with empty values last. On PostgreSQL, grouping spans into time buckets should be exact and handle timestamps before the epoch (negative values) correctly, including at nanosecond boundaries and at the extreme ends of the integer range. Rollup eligibility checks should look only at the traces that contribute to each rollup, and checking whether span costs exist should be a cheap existence check instead of a count. On PostgreSQL, the span-cost grouping queries should be combined into one, and finding candidate days for rollups should use efficient timestamp lookups. Through all of this, workspace isolation, inactivity checks across days, partition locking, and the order in which rollups are published must behave exactly as before.

request: When validating a candidate model against a baseline, the minimum relative change threshold gives wrong results if the baseline metric value is negative. For example, with a baseline R² of -1.8 and a 5% required improvement, a clearly worse candidate at -5.0 passes validation, while a perfect candidate at 1.0 fails. The relative change is currently computed by dividing the difference by the signed baseline value, which flips the direction of the comparison for negative baselines. The relative change should instead be measured against the magnitude (absolute value) of the baseline, for both metrics where higher is better and metrics where lower is better. Behavior for positive baselines must stay exactly the same, and the existing zero-baseline handling (falling back to a plain comparison) must not change. The documentation describing the threshold should also be corrected to state the required value as the baseline plus the relative change times the baseline's magnitude (and the lower-is-better counterpart), noting that this matches the old formula when the baseline is positive.

request: Text I save as an artifact with the text-logging feature is stored as UTF-8. But when I read it back with the text-loading and dictionary-loading artifact functions, they use the machine's default encoding instead. On systems where that default isn't UTF-8 (for example a Traditional Chinese Windows locale), non-ASCII content comes back silently wrong. "café résumé" turns into "caf矇 r矇sum矇". In other cases loading the text fails with "Unable to form a str object from file content", or loading a dictionary fails with a decoding error. Both functions should always read artifacts as UTF-8, so what I logged is what I get back whatever the system locale is. If an artifact isn't valid UTF-8, such as a file in a legacy code page uploaded as a plain artifact file, reading it should fail with a clear error. The error should say the artifact is not valid UTF-8 and suggest downloading the artifact instead, and it should keep the original decoding error as its cause. The dictionary loader should raise that same clear error, not let a raw decoding error escape.

Converting a dataset into an evaluation dataset fails with an error when the dataset contains nested arrays of varying lengths whose elements are dictionaries. For example, a Hugging Face dataset where each row holds a list of dictionaries, and the lists differ in length from row to row. The failure happens while the dataset's content is being hashed (fingerprinted). The hashing step tries to turn the irregular nested data into a uniform rectangular array, and that is impossible when lengths differ, so a value error is raised and the conversion aborts. Datasets with uniform, regular shapes work fine. Converting such datasets should succeed instead of raising an error. When the data can't be made into a uniform array and contains dictionaries, hashing should fall back to a general approach that walks through the nested contents item by item. Hashing should still produce a consistent result, so the same data gives the same hash every time.

When I send a chat request to a Gemini or Vertex AI gateway endpoint with a tool choice setting, the setting is silently ignored. If I require the model to call a tool, force a specific named function, or turn off tool calling entirely, the model still uses Gemini's default automatic tool selection. This happens for both regular and streaming requests. The gateway should honor the setting. "Required" should force the model to call some tool. "None" should prevent any tool call. A specific named function should restrict the model to calling only that function, even when several tools are declared. Omitted or automatic choices should keep today's default behavior. If no tools are declared in the request, no tool-calling configuration should be sent.
